2086.input_message: Now is a good time for BREAKS B=stop and Brake R=Read how your body feels E=Expand and take deep breaths A=Allow everything to be as it is K=Know what's important to you S=take 1 Step in a direction important to you
2086.explanation: Consistent with past Acceptance messages rated Acceptable for content and Moderately helpful for coping/quitting; acronym adds structure for better design.

2087.input_message: Imagine your urge is like a talk radio station going on about something you disagree with. Arguing with it doesn't change what they say. Instead, just let them talk while you focus on what's important to you.
2087.explanation: Similar to past Acceptance messages rated Acceptable in content/design and Moderately helpful in coping/quitting; metaphorical style aligns with participant's prior moderate responses.

2088.input_message: Just because other people are smoking, doesn't mean you have to. Practice allowing this urge to be present for 5 minutes. When it passes, give yourself credit.
2088.explanation: Message is introspective and empowering like the highly rated distraction message, addressing social influences relevant to participant's friends who smoke; acceptance type aligns with moderate motivation and worry traits.

2090.input_message: The best way to deal with any urges from being around smokers is to get out of the situation briefly until it goes. Make an excuse, go to the toilet, go get some water, pretend you need to get some phone reception!
2090.explanation: This message is very similar to the past distraction message about making excuses to leave stressful situations, which was rated poorly across all dimensions.

2089.input_message: Just because letting an urge pass isn't easy, doesn't mean that you can't do it. Try it, you might surprise yourself.
2089.explanation: Encouraging acceptance of urges aligns with the participant's moderate motivation and past high rating for reflective distraction, but as a new Acceptance type, ratings are tempered compared to top distraction message.

2092.input_message: If you find yourself thinking: "I can't do this", "I need a cig", or "I'll just have one", make sure you tell yourself "I absolutely CAN do this", "I'm in control". Take control of your negative thoughts!
2092.explanation: Message similar to highly rated self-reflection distraction (past very good/very helpful), addresses control worries; distraction type aligns with positive past response.

2091.input_message: Did you know that just seeing other people smoke activates a part of your brain that is connected with the action of you smoking? This can bring on strong urges to smoke. One simple solution is to avoid seeing others smoke.
2091.explanation: Similar to the first past distraction message with a practical alternative, but avoidance element echoes the poorly rated third; overall moderate appeal for this moderately motivated participant with some smoking friends.

2093.input_message: Life can get you really stressed out, but turning to cigs isn't the answer. Call or text family and friends instead. Ask them to help you stay on track.
2093.explanation: Message suggests social distraction via family/friends, aligning with participant's somewhat supportive network and moderate motivation; similar to acceptable-rated alternative activity but less introspective than highly rated self-care prompt, so moderately helpful overall.

2094.input_message: Notice what it feels like to see other people smoke and choose not to smoke. Notice what thoughts or emotions come up. Allow them to come and go. They will pass and so will this urge.
2094.explanation: Message encourages mindful acceptance of emotions and urges, similar to the highly rated introspective distraction message; aligns with participant's frequent emotional and worry issues, likely seen as helpful for coping and quitting despite being Acceptance type.

2095.input_message: Some people find that having a simple mantra can really help, especially if things feel stressful. Try repeating something simple to yourself like: "I can do it!".
2095.explanation: This Distraction message uses positive self-talk similar to the participant's positively rated Distraction example, leading to consistent moderate ratings.

2096.input_message: What can you do right now to break the automatic habit of smoking when you are here? Pause. Close your eyes. And take 10 slow breaths.
2096.explanation: As an Acceptance-type message similar to past ones rated Acceptable for content/design and Not at all helpful for coping/quitting, consistent low ratings expected despite motivation to quit.

2097.input_message: Have confidence in knowing that you can have this urge, choose not to smoke, be okay, and choose to do things that matter most to you.
2097.explanation: Participant consistently rates Acceptance messages as Acceptable in content/design and Not at all helpful for coping/quitting, unlike Distraction messages; new message aligns with prior Acceptance examples.

2098.input_message: It's normal to have some doubts during a quit attempt. Keep your quit reasons on hand to remind yourself if ever you feel uncertain or undecided.
2098.explanation: As a Distraction message similar to the positively rated past Distraction example (motivational self-reminder), consistent with participant's preference for Distraction over Acceptance and high quit motivation.

2099.input_message: Try to stop smoking by setting yourself a rule. For example, "IF I am tempted, THEN I will chew on some mints" - make your own rule that will work for you.
2099.explanation: As a highly motivated young smoker with low daily intake, this practical distraction strategy aligns with the positively rated prior distraction message, warranting similar 'Good' content/design and 'Somewhat helpful' for coping/quitting, unlike low-rated acceptance messages.

2100.input_message: Did you know that just seeing other people smoke activates a part of your brain that is connected with the action of you smoking? This can bring on strong urges to smoke. One simple solution is to avoid seeing others smoke.
2100.explanation: Participant rated Distraction messages positively in past (Good content/design, Somewhat helpful coping/quitting) compared to Acceptance; new message is practical Distraction advice aligning with low smoking frequency and high motivation.

2101.input_message: You were often stressed in this location and this might trigger urges. What can you do to reduce your stress here? If you can avoid this place until things settle down, then do.
2101.explanation: As a motivated low-level smoker who rated the prior Distraction message positively (Good content/design, Somewhat helpful), this practical trigger-avoidance advice aligns similarly, unlike unhelpful Acceptance messages.
